body.heading: Design it together first
paragraphs: Before moving anything, sketch the course on paper. A good course has five or six stations and a mix of skills: something to crawl under, something to balance on, something to jump over, something to carry, and a finish line worth sprinting to.
Keep it simple and changeable. A course that can be rearranged in two minutes will be played with far longer than a perfect one that is fixed in place.

body.heading: Build, race, redesign
paragraphs: Lay out the stations with what you already have: a rope on the ground to walk along, cushions to hop between, a bucket to toss a ball into, a chair to crawl under, a garden hose coiled as a slalom. Time each run with a phone stopwatch, and let everyone have a go at beating their own best time rather than each other's.

The best part comes after the first race: ask everyone which station to swap, move or make harder. A course that the players redesign themselves never gets boring, and the redesigning is half the game.

description: Turn cushions, rope, buckets and a garden hose into a wobbly, wonderful obstacle course — then race it, time it, and redesign it together.

materials: A length of rope or a garden hose
A bucket and a soft ball
Chalk or tape for a start and finish line
safetyNotes: Use soft, stable items only — nothing heavy, sharp, or likely to topple onto a player.
Keep the course on flat, clear ground away from roads, fences and hard edges.
Check the ground for stones, wet patches and trip hazards before the first run.
supervision: An adult sets up and supervises throughout, checking that nothing can tip over or cause a hard fall.
takeaway: Five simple stations, a stopwatch and a redesign round turn an ordinary garden into an afternoon of play.
